title: Anthropic locks out Claude users after infostealers hijack login sessions
subtitle: Vidar, Lumma, RedLine, StealC and Atomic Stealer variants pulled active Claude session cookies off infected PCs and burned through paid usage before Anthropic revoked the tokens.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic began signing affected Claude users out of their accounts this weekend after confirming that infostealer malware on user devices had scraped active Claude session cookies and used them to hijack accounts. The company said it is wiping saved payment methods on affected accounts and refunding charges it identifies as unauthorized. Anthropic named Vidar, Lumma (LummaC2), StealC, RedLine and Acreed on Windows, and Atomic Stealer (AMOS) on a small number of Macs, as the malware families used in the campaign.

Session-cookie theft matters because it sidesteps two-factor authentication entirely — the attacker walks in with a valid, already-authenticated browser token and never sees a login prompt. Once inside, the intruder can spend the account's paid usage, pull chat history, and — until the token is revoked — persist through password changes. That is why Anthropic's remediation is to invalidate the session and force a fresh login, not just prompt for a new password.

This is the second Claude-adjacent malware incident in six weeks. In late July, victims searching Bing for 'Claude desktop app' were served sponsored ads pointing to a spoofed download page; roughly 7,100 downloads were served in two days before Anthropic and the ad network took it down, with at least 29 organizations reporting compromise. The pattern — malicious ads, spoofed installers, cookie theft — is the same playbook infostealer crews have run against banks and crypto exchanges for years, now retargeted at AI subscriptions because paid AI usage has real dollar value on the resale market.

For learners: the vulnerable surface is not Claude itself — it is your browser's cookie jar and whatever you installed last week. Only download desktop AI apps from the vendor's own domain (never from a search-ad link), keep the browser's session store isolated from unknown extensions, and if a paid AI plan starts showing usage you did not generate, revoke sessions first and change the password second.
